text.arabic_uthmani: ۞ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا تَتَّخِذُوا۟ ٱلْيَهُودَ وَٱلنَّصَٰرَىٰٓ أَوْلِيَآءَ ۘ بَعْضُهُمْ أَوْلِيَآءُ بَعْضٍۢ ۚ وَمَن يَتَوَلَّهُم مِّنكُمْ فَإِنَّهُۥ مِنْهُمْ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهْدِى ٱلْقَوْمَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ

words.gloss_range: formal vocative opening that summons a qualified audience into a legal directive
words.prose: {{ar:يَا}} ({{tr:yā}}) opens the ayah as formal address before any prohibition is heard. The call gathers the audience, then the ayah moves through prohibition, rationale, conditional consequence, and divine closure, so the legal command is framed as a staged identity warning rather than an isolated rule. The elongated vocative pacing also lets the summons land before the sharp negative command begins.

topics.headline: vocative legal address
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the prohibition is spoken to a summoned and qualified audience before the command itself appears.
topics.reason: The vocative particle begins the address frame, and the following relative clause and prohibition show that the call governs a legal directive to the believing audience.

topics.headline: staged legal architecture
topics.reader_payoff: The reader tracks a sequence from address to command, rationale, consequence, and divine principle.
topics.reason: The attachment profile divides the ayah into vocative qualification, prohibition, nominal rationale, conditional result, and final emphatic declaration.

topics.headline: formal summons before prohibition
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the opening as ceremonially slowed before the clipped prohibition arrives.
topics.reason: The row points to the recited opening pace, and nothing in the local syntax blocks treating it as a formal audible entry into the prohibition.

words.gloss_range: vocative pronoun that holds an open address slot until the relative clause qualifies it
words.prose: {{ar:أَيُّهَا}} ({{tr:ayyuhā}}) keeps the call open before it is narrowed by the relative phrase that follows. The construction does not name a tribe or fixed social label at the outset; it creates an alerted address slot, then lets prior faith-commitment define who is being summoned.

topics.headline: open vocative slot
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the audience is opened broadly and only then qualified by faith.
topics.reason: The vocative pronoun is appositionally specified by the following relative pronoun, so the address waits for its qualifier.

words.gloss_range: relative pronoun that turns the vocative into an identity-qualified address
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلَّذِينَ}} ({{tr:alladhīna}}) supplies the qualifier that completes the vocative. It makes the addressees those defined by the following completed act of faith, so the later prohibition falls on a community already described by commitment, not on an ethnic or geographic category.

topics.headline: relative qualification of the audience
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the legal command is addressed to people defined by prior commitment.
topics.reason: The relative pronoun functions as the appositional qualifier of the vocative and introduces the clause that defines the addressee.

words.gloss_range: completed plural faith or trust-commitment that qualifies the addressed community
words.root_gloss_range: security, trust, faith, and entrusted covenant; local Form IV selects entered trust-commitment as the address qualification
words.prose: {{ar:ءَامَنُوا۟}} ({{tr:āmanū}}) completes the opening qualification as a perfect plural: the hearers are addressed as a formed community already marked by trust-commitment. The root's security and trust range gives the later walāya warning covenantal weight, while the Form IV perfect keeps the local sense on entered faith rather than an abstract root inventory. The word also turns the previous third-person critique of alternative judgment into direct responsibility for this addressed community, and it stands inside a Surah 5 pattern where believers are warned here and then given the proper walī axis in 5:55.

topics.headline: formed trust-commitment community
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the prohibition addresses a community already constituted by trust, so forbidden walāya threatens that identity.
topics.reason: The perfect Form IV plural supports completed communal faith or trust-commitment; broader security and trust associations remain relevant as pressure but do not replace the local faith sense.

topics.headline: completed plural qualification
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees a completed communal identity placed before the future-facing prohibition.
topics.reason: The 3mp perfect ending and clause position make the faith action a completed qualifier for the addressed group.

topics.headline: faith address before proper walī definition
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can place the warning before the nearby positive definition of rightful walāya in 5:55.
topics.reason: Surah-local recurrence links the faith address here with nearby walāya material, especially the positive definition in 5:55.

topics.headline: prior critique becomes direct address
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices a shift from third-person critique into direct responsibility for the believing audience.
topics.reason: The boundary evidence supports a discourse shift from the previous ayah's critique into this ayah's direct vocative prohibition.

words.gloss_range: prohibitive negator governing the action and its two-object role assignment
words.prose: {{ar:لَا}} ({{tr:lā}}) is the prohibitive particle, so it performs a legal boundary rather than merely reporting a fact. Its scope reaches the verb, the named dyad, and the role assigned to them, while the later negator before guidance changes register from command to divine judgment.

topics.headline: prohibitive scope over role assignment
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the barred act is taking the named groups into a specific walī role.
topics.reason: QAC and attachment evidence identify the particle as prohibitive and connect it to the following jussive verb with two complements.

topics.headline: command negator before judgment negator
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the ayah move from a human prohibition to a divine non-guidance statement.
topics.reason: The first negator is prohibitive, while the later one is simple negation over the guidance verb.

words.gloss_range: deliberate adoption in a prohibited double-object construction
words.root_gloss_range: taking, seizing, adopting, and taking for oneself; local Form VIII selects deliberate self-adoption of a role

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: the walī role assigned as the second object of the prohibited adoption

words.prose: {{ar:تَتَّخِذُوا۟}} ({{tr:tattakhidhū}}) carries the prohibition as a jussive verb with two objects: the named groups are the object adopted, and {{ar:أَوْلِيَآءَ}} ({{tr:awliyāʾa}}) is the role assigned to them. The Form VIII shape turns simple taking into deliberate self-adoption, so the ayah targets a chosen patronage relation, not incidental contact. Its recurrence with the same prohibition formula in 5:57 keeps this word inside a local alliance-warning sequence.

topics.headline: double-object role assignment
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the grammar forbids assigning a walī role to the named groups, not merely mentioning them.
topics.reason: The verb is governed by prohibitive negation and takes the named dyad plus the walī plural as two accusative complements.

topics.headline: deliberate self-adoption
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the forbidden act as a chosen adoption into one's own sphere.
topics.reason: The Form VIII jussive under prohibition licenses deliberate adoption or taking for oneself as the local force.

topics.headline: recurring alliance prohibition
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can connect this command with the renewed alliance warning in 5:57.
topics.reason: The same prohibition pattern recurs nearby in 5:57, making the local verb part of a repeated Surah 5 warning.

words.gloss_range: definite named collective as the first governed object in the prohibited dyad
words.root_gloss_range: group name with a debated relation to returning or repenting; locally the named collective sense is selected while return imagery is secondary

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: the second definite group coordinated into the same prohibited dyad

words.prose: {{ar:ٱلْيَهُودَ}} ({{tr:al-yahūda}}) is the first definite collective object of the prohibited adoption, coordinated with {{ar:ٱلنَّصَٰرَىٰٓ}} ({{tr:al-naṣārā}}). The disputed return-root background is narrowed here: the local word names a recognized community, yet the later turning verb lets the return or turning pressure remain audible as a secondary irony. Surah 5 repeatedly profiles this named group, and here the profile becomes a rule about believers' walāya toward the dyad.

topics.headline: definite first object in the dyad
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees a recognized collective placed under the same prohibited role as the following coordinated group.
topics.reason: The word is definite and accusative as the first object of the prohibited adoption verb.

topics.headline: return-root tension under turning language
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices a directional tension: a name linked with return appears inside a warning about where believers must not turn.
topics.reason: The derivation is contested, so the local group-name sense controls; the later walāya verb allows the return or turning association as secondary pressure only.

topics.headline: Surah 5 dyad profile
topics.reader_payoff: The reader places the term within a concentrated Surah 5 profile where the dyad appears in claims, critique, and relational assessment.
topics.reason: Contextual evidence links the term with repeated Surah 5 occurrences and with the paired group formula, including 5:18 and 5:82.

words.gloss_range: coordinating conjunction that binds the second group into the same prohibited object complex
words.prose: {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}) joins the second named group to the first under one prohibition. The conjunction makes the target cumulative rather than sequential: the dyad shares the same verb, the same negative scope, and the same prohibited walī role.

topics.headline: coordinated dyad under one prohibition
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the two named groups treated as one governed object-complex for this legal warning.
topics.reason: The conjunction coordinates the two group names inside the same object slot under the same prohibitive verb.

words.gloss_range: definite coordinated community name with help-root pressure under the prohibited walī role
words.root_gloss_range: help, support, victory, and named communal identity; locally the group-name sense is selected while help-language colors the prohibited support relation
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلنَّصَٰرَىٰٓ}} ({{tr:al-naṣārā}}) shares objecthood with the first group and is not an afterthought. Its help-root background is narrowed by the definite collective form: the word names a community, not generic helpers, but that background sharpens the warning because a help-associated name is placed inside a prohibition about taking awliyāʾ. The same n-ṣ-r helper field also brushes against anṣār language, making the support collision more pointed while the local referent remains the named community. Surah 5 then keeps this group-name in a broader covenantal and relational profile.

topics.headline: second coordinated object
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the second group shares the same accusative governance and legal role as the first.
topics.reason: The word is coordinated to the first object and appears as a definite collective group-name under the same verb.

topics.headline: help-root contrast in a prohibited support role
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the semantic tension between help-language and the barred support structure.
topics.reason: The local word is a community name, so help or victory cannot replace the selected sense; it can still sharpen the contrast with forbidden walāya support.

topics.headline: Surah 5 group profile
topics.reader_payoff: The reader places the group-name inside a recurring Surah 5 profile rather than treating it as a one-off label.
topics.reason: Contextual evidence links the group name with Surah 5 covenantal, salvation, and relational contexts and with the dyad formula.

words.gloss_range: accusative second object naming the prohibited role of ally, protector, patron, or authority-near figure
words.root_gloss_range: nearness, succession, guardianship, protection, patronage, alliance, and authority; local role includes more than casual friendship
words.prose: {{ar:أَوْلِيَآءَ}} ({{tr:awliyāʾa}}) names what the groups are not to be made into. As the second object, it specifies the prohibited role, and the w-l-y field carries nearness into protection, patronage, and authority, so the warning cannot be flattened into casual friendship; the reported arbāban variant tests that vertical authority endpoint without displacing the standard wording. The broken plural makes the role networked, and the same plural returns as a predicate in the rationale; nearby 5:55 then gives the proper walī axis that answers this improper one.

topics.headline: prohibited walī role
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the prohibition concerns authority-near protection and patronage, not ordinary social warmth alone.
topics.reason: The word is the second object of the adoption verb, and the lexical evidence supports a range from nearness and friendship to guardianship and authority.

topics.headline: plural network echoed in the rationale
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the prohibited role return as the reason: they already form awliyāʾ networks among themselves.
topics.reason: The broken plural first appears as an accusative complement and then recurs as a nominative predicate in the following nominal sentence.

topics.headline: improper role answered by 5:55
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can see 5:55 as the positive definition that follows this negative boundary.
topics.reason: Surah-local evidence contrasts the improper awliyāʾ role here with the proper walī relation named in 5:55.

words.gloss_range: partitive subject with a pronoun tying the reciprocal clause back to the prohibited dyad
words.root_gloss_range: part, portion, some of a whole; locally used for internal segmentation within the named dyad
words.prose: {{ar:بَعْضُهُمْ}} ({{tr:baʿḍuhum}}) begins the rationale as a partitive subject with its pronoun tied back to the named dyad. The nominal sentence makes their mutual walāya a standing internal structure, not a temporary event. The same reciprocal formula can mark legitimate believer walāya in 8:72, so here the payoff is not anti-reciprocity in general but the wrong communal patronage network; the repeated -hum sound also threads this internal network into the later act and membership verdict.

topics.headline: standing reciprocal network
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the rationale names a standing internal alliance structure among the prohibited referents.
topics.reason: The word is the subject of a verbless reciprocal sentence whose pronoun refers back to the coordinated dyad.

topics.headline: pronoun tether to the dyad
topics.reader_payoff: The reader keeps the reciprocal statement tied to the named groups rather than generalizing it away.
topics.reason: The attached third-person plural suffix routes the partitive noun back to the prohibited dyad.

topics.headline: reciprocal formula contrasted with 8:72
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the problem is adopting the wrong network, not reciprocal solidarity as such.
topics.reason: The same reciprocal structure appears for believers in 8:72, which narrows the local warning to wrong referents and wrong walāya.

topics.headline: pronoun sound thread
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the pronoun chain link internal alliance, turning to them, and final membership.
topics.reason: The repeated third-person plural suffix is locally visible across the reciprocal statement, the conditional verb, and the membership phrase.

words.gloss_range: nominative predicate asserting the dyad's existing internal walāya
words.root_gloss_range: nearness, alliance, protection, patronage, and authority; locally predicate names an existing reciprocal role
words.prose: {{ar:أَوْلِيَآءُ}} ({{tr:awliyāʾu}}) repeats the same plural from the prohibition but changes its case and function. The first occurrence was the role believers must not assign; this nominative predicate states what the dyad already is internally. That grammar makes the command's logic visible: do not adopt them as awliyāʾ because their own walāya network is already active.

topics.headline: predicate internal walāya
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the rationale asserts an existing internal patronage relation.
topics.reason: The word is nominative as the predicate of a verbless sentence, assigning walāya as a standing attribute.

topics.headline: case-shift echo from command to rationale
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the same plural move from prohibited assigned role to descriptive reality.
topics.reason: The repetition across different case roles links the prohibition to its explanatory clause.

words.gloss_range: genitive reciprocal endpoint completing the internal part-to-part relation
words.root_gloss_range: part, portion, some of a whole; locally completes the distributive endpoint of reciprocity
words.prose: {{ar:بَعْضٍۢ}} ({{tr:baʿḍin}}) completes the reciprocal construction as the genitive endpoint: some of them are awliyāʾ of some. The indefinite genitive keeps the endpoint distributive rather than fixed, and the repeated partitive root makes the internal loop audible as well as grammatical.

topics.headline: reciprocal endpoint
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the predicate completed as a part-to-part relation inside the same collective.
topics.reason: The genitive partitive noun completes the reciprocal relation after the predicate plural.

topics.headline: self-enclosed reciprocal loop
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the repeated partitive root close the alliance circuit inside the same group field.
topics.reason: The same partitive root appears at both ends of the nominal clause with different case and attachment.

words.gloss_range: resumptive connector moving from rationale to conditional consequence
words.prose: {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}) resumes the discourse after the reciprocal rationale and opens the conditional warning. It does not add another item to the dyad; it links the explanation to the next legal consequence, so the argument remains continuous while the clause type changes.

topics.headline: rationale to conditional consequence
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the ayah turning from explanation to consequence without breaking the argument.
topics.reason: The conjunction precedes the conditional particle and links the prior nominal rationale to the following protasis and apodosis.

words.gloss_range: conditional particle universalizing the violation while individualizing accountability
words.prose: {{ar:مَن}} ({{tr:man}}) turns the prohibition into a conditional case: whoever from the addressed community performs the walāya act falls under the consequence. The shift from second-person plural command to third-person singular condition individualizes accountability while the following phrase keeps the risk inside the believing audience.

topics.headline: universal conditional risk
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the command converted into a repeatable legal test for any violator.
topics.reason: The particle introduces the conditional protasis that triggers the following apodosis.

topics.headline: individualized internal accountability
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the external problem can become an internal defection by any one member of the addressed group.
topics.reason: The discourse shifts from plural address to singular conditional while the following source phrase locates the risk among the addressees.

words.gloss_range: Form V conditional verb: self-directed turning into their walāya with the prohibited dyad as object
words.root_gloss_range: nearness, alliance, protection, authority, taking as walī, turning toward, and turning away; local form selects self-positioning toward them as the condition trigger
words.prose: {{ar:يَتَوَلَّهُم}} ({{tr:yatawallahum}}) is the conditional trigger: if someone takes their walāya, the membership verdict follows. The bound -hum keeps the prohibited dyad as the object of the act and prepares the later membership phrase. Form V makes the subject self-enter the relation, while the root's toward-away range makes that entry also a departure from the proper walāya order; 5:56 reverses the object by naming the proper side of this same verb field. The verb also makes the prior governance disorder concrete as personal allegiance, and 5:52 displays that misdirected movement as visible behavior.

topics.headline: walāya act as condition trigger
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the identity verdict triggered specifically by turning to the prohibited dyad as walī object.
topics.reason: The jussive verb stands in the conditional protasis and carries a third-person plural object suffix referring to the named dyad.

topics.headline: self-directed turning and departure
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the act as self-positioning toward one side and away from the proper community boundary.
topics.reason: The Form V morphology supports self-directed involvement, and the lexical range includes taking as walī and turning; the local object keeps the selected sense tied to prohibited walāya rather than generic turning.

topics.headline: proper and prohibited walāya contrasted
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can contrast this object of turning with the proper object of walāya named in 5:56.
topics.reason: Surah-local evidence places this verb against the positive walāya statement in 5:56 and the surrounding warning sequence.

topics.headline: wrong governance becomes visible alliance
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the conditional as the mechanism by which a prior governance disorder becomes concrete allegiance behavior, which 5:52 then displays.
topics.reason: Boundary evidence links the previous judgment theme to this walāya condition and forward to the next ayah's visible rushing behavior.

words.gloss_range: partitive source phrase locating the possible violator inside the addressed audience
words.prose: {{ar:مِّنكُمْ}} ({{tr:minkum}}) prevents the warning from being externalized. The preposition with the second-person plural suffix marks a subset from among the addressed believers, making the risk internal to the very community summoned at the opening.

topics.headline: internal source group
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the conditional danger arises from within the addressed believers, not only outside them.
topics.reason: The partitive preposition plus second-person plural suffix refers back to the vocative audience.

topics.headline: external critique pulled inward
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the previous external disorder become a live risk inside the addressed group.
topics.reason: Boundary evidence supports the pronoun phrase as a hinge from earlier external critique into current internal warning.

words.gloss_range: result particle introducing the conditional apodosis as immediate logical consequence
words.prose: {{ar:فَ}} ({{tr:fa}}) is the hinge from condition to verdict. It marks the following assertion as the answer to the conditional, so turning to them does not merely precede reclassification; it directly triggers the emphatic identity consequence.

topics.headline: result hinge into identity verdict
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the walāya act converted immediately into a membership verdict.
topics.reason: The particle introduces the conditional answer and combines with the emphatic clause that follows.

topics.headline: result plus emphatic assertion
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the consequence stated with both logical and rhetorical force.
topics.reason: The apodosis begins with result particle plus emphatic particle rather than a bare pronoun.

words.gloss_range: emphatic singular subject of the apodosis, individuating the violator in an identity assertion
words.prose: {{ar:إِنَّهُۥ}} ({{tr:innahū}}) compresses emphasis and singular accountability into the result clause. The pronoun points back to whoever violates the condition, while the emphatic construction makes the consequence an identity assertion: not merely that he acted like them, but that he is counted of them.

topics.headline: singular accountability in the verdict
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that a universal condition lands on an individual actor.
topics.reason: The singular pronoun refers back to the conditional particle rather than the plural groups.

topics.headline: emphatic membership assertion
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the apodosis as reinforced reclassification rather than a loose comparison.
topics.reason: The standard construction fuses result, emphatic assertion, and pronoun, producing a nominal identity verdict.

words.gloss_range: classificatory membership phrase with pronoun referring to the prohibited dyad
words.prose: {{ar:مِنْهُمْ}} ({{tr:minhum}}) completes the verdict with membership, not physical origin. The same prepositional shape has just marked a person from among the addressed believers, and now the pronoun changes to them: the grammar makes the transfer from among you to of them visible and audible.

topics.headline: classificatory membership verdict
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the consequence as belonging and classification, not mere proximity.
topics.reason: The preposition plus third-person plural suffix functions locally as a predicate of membership in the apodosis.

topics.headline: from-you to of-them transfer
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the same prepositional frame switch pronouns to enact group transfer.
topics.reason: The paired phrases share the same preposition and cadence while changing from the second-person audience to the third-person prohibited dyad.

words.gloss_range: emphatic particle opening the final divine closure after the conditional verdict
words.prose: {{ar:إِنَّ}} ({{tr:inna}}) opens a second emphatic clause, shifting from the human membership consequence to a divine closing principle. The repeated emphatic particle links the verdict that he is of them with the statement that God does not guide the wrongdoing people. It also connects the warning sequence to nearby Surah 5 contrasts: walāya is positively defined in 5:55-56, and guidance is granted or withheld across 5:16 and 5:51.

topics.headline: emphatic divine closure
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the ayah move from conditional reclassification to a categorical divine principle.
topics.reason: The second emphatic particle begins the final independent closure and echoes the earlier emphatic apodosis.

topics.headline: walāya and guidance contrasts nearby
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can read the closure alongside nearby positive walāya and guidance statements in Surah 5.
topics.reason: The rows provide concrete Surah 5 contrasts with walāya redirection in 5:55-56 and positive guidance in 5:16.

words.gloss_range: divine name governed by the final emphatic particle and placed as the subject of the closing principle
words.root_gloss_range: proper divine name with worship, divinity, refuge, and authority associations; locally names God as agent of non-guidance and true authority over walāya
words.prose: {{ar:ٱللَّهَ}} ({{tr:Allāha}}) is placed at the head of the final emphatic clause as the divine agent of the guidance verdict. In a context saturated with w-l-y language, the name reframes the dispute over protectors and authority: misplaced walāya seeks refuge and patronage where ultimate authority belongs to God, and 5:55 makes that proper walī axis explicit. The syntax therefore lets the closure govern the whole preceding alliance sequence.

topics.headline: divine agent of the closing verdict
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees divine agency placed at the head of the closing principle.
topics.reason: The divine name is accusative as the governed subject of the final emphatic clause, whose predicate is the negated guidance verb.

topics.headline: divine authority and refuge against misplaced walāya
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that forbidden walāya displaces the source of refuge and authority, not merely social association.
topics.reason: The local proper name selects God as subject; worship, refuge, and authority associations survive as pressure because the ayah's central issue is misplaced walāya.

topics.headline: Surah 5 legal authority profile
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can place the closure in Surah 5's repeated pattern of divine authority, walāya, and guidance.
topics.reason: Contextual evidence links the divine name with guidance and walāya fields and with repeated Surah 5 legal authority language.

words.gloss_range: simple negator over the guidance verb in the final divine statement
words.prose: {{ar:لَا}} ({{tr:lā}}) here is simple negation, not prohibition. It scopes specifically over the guidance verb, so the closure does not make an undefined denial about God; it states that the wrongdoing people are not guided. The second negator turns the earlier legal boundary into a generalizing guidance principle.

topics.headline: negation scoped to guidance
topics.reader_payoff: The reader distinguishes the final negation of guidance from the opening prohibition of action.
topics.reason: QAC identifies this particle as simple negation over the imperfect guidance verb, unlike the earlier prohibitive negator.

topics.headline: generalizing non-guidance formula
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the specific alliance violation carried into an enduring principle about misdirected loyalty and guidance.
topics.reason: The final clause takes the specific warning and closes it with a categorical statement about a defined wrongdoing people.

words.gloss_range: negated imperfect guidance verb with explicit object, presenting an ongoing divine non-guidance principle
words.root_gloss_range: guiding, leading, showing the way, and giving as a gift; locally guidance is withheld from the specified wrongdoing people
words.prose: {{ar:يَهْدِى}} ({{tr:yahdī}}) is an imperfect verb under negation with its object present, so the closure is targeted rather than elliptical. Its guidance root gives the verdict path imagery: wrong walāya becomes a loss of divine orientation. The gift branch adds the sense of withheld bestowal, while 5:16 shows the same surah's positive guidance contrast and 5:67 shows a related non-guidance formula with a different qualifier. The next ayah's exposed rush among them in 5:52 then gives the non-guidance verdict a behavioral surface.

topics.headline: targeted ongoing non-guidance
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees non-guidance as an ongoing principle aimed at an explicit object class.
topics.reason: The imperfect verb is negated, has God as subject, and takes the following definite noun phrase as its explicit object.

topics.headline: path orientation and withheld gift
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the closure as denied orientation and withheld divine bestowal for a group whose loyalty is misplaced.
topics.reason: The local verb selects guidance; the root's giving branch remains a secondary image because negation frames guidance as something not granted.

topics.headline: Surah guidance contrasts
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can contrast positive guidance in 5:16 with the negative formula here and related non-guidance wording in 5:67.
topics.reason: The formula recurs with different qualifiers, so the contrast is formulaic and thematic; it should not collapse the distinct labels into a single identical category.

topics.headline: non-guidance echoed by next behavior
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the closing non-guidance answered by the next ayah's exposed misdirected movement in 5:52.
topics.reason: The next ayah shows behavior that fits the loss of orientation named in the closure.

words.gloss_range: definite singular collective object of non-guidance, forming a recognized people-class with its adjective
words.root_gloss_range: standing, rising, establishing, uprightness, collective peoplehood, and accountability; locally the collective people-class is selected
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلْقَوْمَ}} ({{tr:al-qawma}}) is the explicit object of the negated guidance verb. As a definite singular collective, it turns the consequence from one violator alone into a recognized people-class once modified by the following adjective. The q-w-m standing field gives that class a posture of collective alignment, and Surah 5 sharpens the contrast by moving from the people of certainty in 5:50 to the wrongdoing people here.

topics.headline: definite collective object
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the closure targets a recognized collective class, not only the singular conditional actor.
topics.reason: The word is accusative as object of the guidance verb and definite as a singular collective modified by the following adjective.

topics.headline: standing collective pressure
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the people-class as a collective standing in a morally displaced alignment.
topics.reason: The local noun means people or community; broader standing and accountability associations add pressure without replacing that selected sense.

topics.headline: guidance and wrongdoing pairing
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the collective noun pulled between the guidance verb and the wrongdoing adjective.
topics.reason: Co-occurrence and grammar place the noun as object of non-guidance and as the head modified by the wrongdoing participle.

topics.headline: people-class contrast with 5:50
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the boundary contrast between a certainty-qualified people in 5:50 and a wrongdoing-qualified people in 5:51.
topics.reason: Boundary and recurrence evidence links the collective noun across nearby legal and communal pivots, especially 5:50 and 5:54.

words.gloss_range: definite active participle adjective classifying the people as wrongdoers marked by misplaced walāya
words.root_gloss_range: wronging, oppression, putting a thing out of place, and darkness; locally wrongdoing and misplacement classify the people in the guidance closure
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ}} ({{tr:al-ẓālimīna}}) locks the moral label onto the people as a definite active participle. The root's misplacement sense makes the closing diagnosis precise: the forbidden walāya puts loyalty, protection, and authority in the wrong place. Darkness imagery can color the negated guidance closure, especially against the positive guidance-light pattern in 5:16, while the active participle presents the group as characterized by an ongoing wrongdoing posture. The governance disorder at 5:50 becomes alliance misplacement here, and the heavy assimilation into emphatic ẓāʾ lets the verdict land audibly.

topics.headline: adjectival moral classification
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees non-guidance aimed at the people specifically as ongoing wrongdoers.
topics.reason: The definite accusative masculine plural participle agrees with the preceding definite collective noun as its adjective.

topics.headline: misplaced walāya diagnosis
topics.reader_payoff: The reader understands the final wrongdoing as misplacing loyalty and authority, not generic injustice detached from the ayah.
topics.reason: The root evidence includes putting something out of place, and the local ayah centers on misdirected walāya.

topics.headline: darkness pressure against guidance
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the non-guidance verdict darkened by the root's darkness association while keeping wrongdoing as the selected label.
topics.reason: Darkness is a related root image and 5:16 supplies a guidance-light contrast, but the local participle selects the moral wrongdoing sense.

topics.headline: Surah 5 judgment-label profile
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can place this label among Surah 5's differentiated judgment terms around revelation, governance, and allegiance.
topics.reason: Surah 5 uses several nearby evaluative labels, and this word marks the walāya warning as part of that broader misplacement category.

topics.headline: boundary diagnosis and audible landing
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears and tracks the final label as the place where the previous governance disorder becomes alliance misplacement.
topics.reason: The boundary evidence links the prior disorder to this closing label, and the phonetic row highlights the emphatic assimilated landing of the final word.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: The paired constructions "do not take ... awliya" and "whoever takes them in wilaya" make the relation an object of deliberate adoption.
baseline_models.mechanism: Taking/acquiring installs a wilaya relation whose live range includes close attachment, support, and standing over affairs. The noun is repeated and then converted into the subject's act, so the warning concerns chosen dependence or delegated patronage rather than mere coexistence.

activation_trace.role: The image of making or acquiring something for oneself makes the patronal relation an installed choice.
Standing over and managing an affair supplies the governing or custodial side of the adopted relation.
Love, aid, and alliance supply the supportive side of wilaya without reducing it to private sentiment.

changed_reading.before: A general ban on friendly feeling toward the two named communities.
changed_reading.after: A ban on deliberately installing their communal actors or networks as patrons, governing allies, or decisive supports.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: The reciprocal "some of them are awliya of some" is followed by "whoever ... among you is from them."
baseline_models.mechanism: Repeated part-to-part language depicts an internally reciprocal network. Wilaya closes the gap between its members and runs continuously through them; entering that relation changes the operative bloc to which the entrant belongs.

activation_trace.role: The part or segment image makes the two reciprocal slots components of a larger alliance arrangement.
Nearness without an intervening gap explains how patronage creates operative adjacency and belonging.
Unbroken succession turns isolated ties into a relay-like network that persists from member to member.

changed_reading.before: "From them" names an already fixed identity.
changed_reading.after: "From them" can name an enacted affiliation: reciprocal patronage composes a bloc, and volunteering into its chain effects practical membership.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: Believers are addressed before the adopted wilaya, and the ayah closes by denying guidance to the wrongdoing people.
baseline_models.mechanism: Faith carries security and trust; guidance carries course and direction; wrongdoing can be putting something outside its proper place. Taken together, the prohibited relation misallocates governing trust and thereby bends a collective course.

activation_trace.role: Settled security and trust make the addressees' search for an alternate protective center a live tension.
Direction, course, and habitual way make denied guidance the consequence of a wrongly oriented alliance.
A supporting framework or means of subsistence gives the named people a collective-system dimension.
Putting a thing outside its proper place casts the patronal transfer as a misplacement of trust and authority.

changed_reading.before: The closing non-guidance is a separate judgment appended to an identity rule.
changed_reading.after: The closing judgment diagnoses the mechanism: adopted patronage relocates security and direction, producing a collectively misoriented order.

context_deltas.mechanism: The early pericope counter-scales the focus ayah's reciprocal parts with one life repeatedly valued as all people. This revises bloc membership into an ethical danger when protection of one's part licenses destruction or corruption against the human whole.

activation_trace.role: Partition into reciprocal segments supplies the focus-side pressure toward factional partiality.
Mutual aid and alliance provide the mechanism by which a part can protect its own.
Taking life supplies the concrete terminal harm against which factional protection is measured.
Departure from sound order broadens the harm from a single act to corruption of the common field.
Wholeness without remainder makes every individual life answer to an all-people scale rather than a partisan one.
Preserving life and refraining from killing supplies the positive constraint on alliance behavior.

structural_cues: 5:51 repeats part-to-part reciprocity, while 5:32 repeats one-life/all-people equivalence around killing and saving.
The Cain sequence begins with brotherhood but shows that close relation alone does not secure justice.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies reciprocal parts and an all-human valuation of life; I infer that unjust wilaya is especially the solidarity that lets a part outrank that whole. A live alternative is that 5:32 constrains violence only and does not define patronage generally.

changed_reading.before: Reciprocal in-group support is intrinsically the whole problem.
changed_reading.after: The sharper danger is partisan patronage that makes reciprocal bloc protection override life, sound order, and justice owed beyond the bloc.

context_deltas.mechanism: The judicial pericope depicts words moved from their places, a conditional instruction to take only a favorable ruling, delegation of judgment, and subsequent turning away. These operations activate adopted wilaya as selective jurisdiction: a patron or judge is installed when useful and abandoned when the criterion resists.

activation_trace.role: Deliberate acquisition anchors the changed reading in the focus command against installing a relation.
Standing over an affair makes jurisdiction and governance a live dimension of awliya.
Deviation from a direction supplies the first operation in bending an authoritative criterion.
Putting something in its assigned place makes displacement of words a concrete reordering of authority.
Taking and holding the offered ruling supplies the context's conditional uptake mechanism.
Delegating arbitration supplies the act of placing an authority over a disputed affair.
Turning away after seeking judgment exposes an opportunistic reverse side of wilaya.

structural_cues: 5:41 sequences textual displacement, "if given this, take it," and warning when it is not given.
5:43 sequences seeking delegated judgment, possessing God's judgment, and then turning away.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies selective uptake and reversible adjudication; I infer an arrow from forum-shopping to the focus ayah's adopted patronage. The narrower alternative is that these verses diagnose only legal manipulation, not every form of wilaya.

changed_reading.before: Taking awliya is primarily an affective or social closeness.
changed_reading.after: Taking awliya includes transferring decisive jurisdiction to a network that can reroute judgment through selective uptake and withdrawal.

context_deltas.mechanism: Immediately before the focus, the packet holds together authoritative oversight, resistance to desire, distinct communal paths, a counterfactual single community, and competition in good. Difference is retained as a test while governing orientation remains answerable to revelation; the ban therefore targets transfer of criterion and allegiance, not the bare existence of plural communities.

activation_trace.role: Turning one's face, following, and approving supplies the focus-side transfer of governing orientation.
Witnessing oversight supplies a criterion that can supervise rather than erase prior communities.
The self's inclination supplies the rival directional force that can pull judgment off criterion.
A clear, manifest path makes differentiated communal routing explicit rather than accidental.
A community as a gathered type supplies the plural collective units under discussion.
Union into one direction supplies the unrealized alternative against which plurality is purposeful.
Advancing through competition converts communal difference into forward ethical action.
Inclination toward beneficial good supplies the field in which communities are told to compete.

structural_cues: 5:44 and 5:46 call the Torah and Gospel sites of guidance and light before 5:51 names their communities.
5:48 says each has a law and clear path, declines the single-community counterfactual, names testing, and commands competition in good.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies acknowledged revelations, plural paths, non-unification, and a common ethical race; I infer that 5:51 regulates allegiance across that plurality rather than commanding undifferentiated social erasure. The packet does not settle every ordinary intercommunal relationship.

changed_reading.before: The named communities as such are objects of an undifferentiated social separation.
changed_reading.after: Plural communities remain within the test, but believers must not transfer their governing orientation to communal patronage networks that displace their criterion.

context_deltas.mechanism: The next ayah exposes a crisis calculus: impaired hearts rush into the other network because they fear a reversal of fortune, while an opening or judgment may reverse that wager. Wilaya becomes protective hedging under anticipated power shifts.

activation_trace.role: Security and trust make fear-based outsourcing of protection the focus-side tension.
Aid and alliance provide the protective instrument sought by the fearful entrant.
Speed opposed to deliberation turns affiliation into an urgent move under perceived threat.
Fear with awe supplies the entrants' stated motive for seeking the other network.
Departure from health and balance diagnoses the internal distortion driving the rush.
Circulation of conditions supplies the imagined swing in power against which affiliation is hedged.
Opening what is closed through judgment supplies the event that exposes and reverses the hidden wager.

structural_cues: 5:52 directly follows the prohibition and explains the rush "among them" by fear of a turning calamity.
The feared reversal is answered by a possible opening or command from God and subsequent regret.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies haste, fear, cycling fortune, and a counter-opening; I infer wilaya as a security portfolio chosen for regime risk. "Opening" may be judgment, relief, or victory, but each alternative still overturns the fear-based calculation.

changed_reading.before: The prohibited tie is a stable preference for outsiders.
changed_reading.after: It is especially an opportunistic security hedge: rushing into a patronage network because anticipated power, rather than faith's trust, determines one's decisive support.

context_deltas.mechanism: Those who swore emphatically that they were with the believers are exposed through collapsed deeds. This context makes the focus's movement from "among you" to "from them" operational: enacted alignment can defeat a verbal membership claim.

activation_trace.role: Turning toward, following, and approving supplies the enacted orientation by which belonging changes.
The oath image supplies the strongest verbal claim of being with the believers.
Descent and collapse make the oath's apparent membership fail under exposure.
Intentional action supplies the behavioral register on which the claimed affiliation is tested.

structural_cues: 5:51 says a person can begin "among you" yet become "from them" through tawalli.
5:53 contrasts maximal oaths of being "with you" with deeds that come to nothing.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies opposed membership markers: an oath of being with one group and actions that collapse, beside tawalli that makes one from another group. I infer that operative allegiance outranks self-description; the alternative is that 5:53 concerns a particular hidden cohort only.

changed_reading.before: Communal belonging is secured by profession or declared association.
changed_reading.after: Belonging is tested by the support structure one actually enters: oath and label can say "with you" while tawalli and action make one operationally "from them."

context_deltas.mechanism: The closing pair supplies a positive counter-network: the singular wali relation is assigned to God, the messenger, and practicing believers, then tawalli yields a party organized around God. Prayer, giving, and humility make wilaya embodied practice; party and prevailing power make it collective alignment.

activation_trace.role: The focus branch of aid, affection, and alliance is the relation positively reassigned by the closing ayat.
Standing over and caring for an affair makes the singular positive wali a locus of authority and protection.
Purification and soundness make material giving a visible practice of the counter-wilaya.
Humility and lowered posture prevent the positive alliance from being defined by domination alone.
Actively entering support and alliance converts the positive wali list into a chosen affiliation.
A group organized around a shared position gives tawalli an explicit coalition form.
Prevailing force supplies the collective efficacy promised to this differently ordered alliance.

structural_cues: 5:54 profiles the replacement people by reciprocal love, gentleness toward believers, firmness, striving, and freedom from blame-fear.
5:55 uses an exclusive positive wali construction; 5:56 repeats tawalli and immediately names the resulting party.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the positive wali list, embodied practices, and party outcome; I infer that 5:51 regulates coalition architecture rather than private emotion alone. A live alternative is that the positive construction foregrounds spiritual loyalty without exhausting wilaya's political range.

changed_reading.before: The ayah only removes a relationship and leaves a social vacuum.
changed_reading.after: It redirects patronage into a worshiping, giving, humble, and mutually supporting coalition whose operative center is God, the messenger, and believers.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This is surprising because the cited form is a lexicalized community name, not an instruction to derive its members' function from the root. It remains anchored because the packet supplies the name under the aid root beside awliya's aid branch. Render only as a root-image echo: the attraction of available help may intensify the temptation to promote helpers into decisive patrons.
surprising_valid_outliers.focus_anchor: The proper name al-Nasara stands immediately before awliya in the prohibition.

activation_trace.role: Aid and making another prevail create an exploratory helper-image inside the community name.
Aid and alliance in awliya turn the adjacent helper-image into a temptation to elevate assistance into patronage.

changed_reading.before: The named community and the patronage term contribute unrelated lexical material.
changed_reading.after: As a contained root echo, the verse may expose how the promise of help itself draws a believer toward converting helpers into governing allies.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This is a form-distant activation from the packet's alternate mapped root for h-d-y. It remains anchored to the closing hidaya, qawm, and wrongdoing sequence and forms a coherent support-placement mechanism. Downstream prose must mark it as a cross-map structural image, not as the lexical meaning of "guide": misplaced patronage removes the right supports and leaves the collective order exposed to breaking.
surprising_valid_outliers.focus_anchor: The closing sequence denies hidaya to the wrongdoing qawm after the patronage transfer.

activation_trace.role: Severe breaking or demolition supplies an exploratory negative image behind the denial of guidance.
A supporting framework or mainstay gives the people a structure capable of standing or failing.
Misplacing something supplies the destabilizing act that leaves the collective support system wrongly assembled.

changed_reading.before: Non-guidance is only an epistemic failure to receive direction.
changed_reading.after: Exploratorily, it also images non-stabilization: a people who misplace patronal supports are not carried into a sound course and their collective frame remains liable to break.

strongest_changes: The focus-only friendship reading shifted to deliberate transfer of patronal, supportive, and jurisdictional alignment.
5:41-50 made selective judgment and governing criterion central while intentional communal plurality constrained an undifferentiated separation reading.
5:52 identified fear of changing power as the immediate motive for rushing into the prohibited network.
5:53-56 made belonging operational: deeds can defeat an oath, while positive tawalli produces an embodied coalition.
summary.what_was_special: The trace turned on repeated relational grammar: take awliya, reciprocal part-to-part wilaya, become from them, then a positive wali and party. The context exposed both the hidden risk calculus behind entry and the practices that constitute the counter-network.
remaining_uncertainties: The packet keeps proximity, affection, aid, governance, and coalition live within wilaya but does not select one exhaustive English equivalent.
The plural-path context limits a blanket exclusion reading without fully specifying every ordinary social relation.
The Nasara aid echo and the h-d-d collapse image are deliberately contained branch-distant activations, not lexical conclusions.

reader_a.activated_readings_md: 1. **Assumed charge changes group location.** `و ل ي B003` is assuming authority, `B004` loyal support, and `ب ع ض B001` partitions a whole. Repeated partial-group relations culminate in “he is of them.” I infer that sustained protective allegiance relocates the agent within the social partition it empowers; the ayah targets governing alignment, not mere proximity.
reader_a.retrospective_surprises_md: Later ayah 5:120 made the fixed ayah's local distinctions newly visible as bounded operations within a single encompassing dominion, rather than as an isolated rule or episode.

reader_a.activated_readings_md: 1. **Wilāyah is identity-shaping alignment.** Repeated fixed **و ل ي / B004** (“loyal alliance and support”) combines with **B006** (“turning toward and facing”) in *yatawallahum*. The prior window concerns whose judgment directs conduct; 5:52 shows diseased hearts rushing into this alignment, while 5:55–5:56 name an alternative *walī* and its gathered party. I infer that sustained facing, support, and delegated charge make a person functionally part of the aligned body. “He is of them” thus reads as relational incorporation, not a claim that ordinary contact erases every distinction.
reader_a.retrospective_surprises_md: 5:52 displayed the rushing incorporation, while 5:55–5:56 supplied an alternative *walī* relation whose practices gather a different party.

identity_judgment.rationale: Kaynak ifadeleri bu dali yalniz korkunun kalkmasi olarak degil, kalbin yatismasi, guven verme, guvenilirlik, emanet edilen sey, guvenli yer ve dayanilir nitelik alanlariyla birlikte verir. Bu nedenle dalin cercevesi, guvenlik ve guvenilirlik ekseninde hem yalın hem de yapimli ve baglamli kullanislari ayirt ederek korunabilir.

lexicalization_scope.note: Yalin guven ve korkusuzluk anlamlari ile belirli yapimli ya da soz obegi kullanislari birlikte vardir; tanim bunlari tek bir dar kaliba indirgemez.

concept_map.definition: Korkunun kalkmasiyla kalbin yatismasi, birine guven verilmesi veya bir kimsenin ya da seyin guvenilir kabul edilmesidir. Bu alan guvenli yer, emanet edilen sey, kendisine guvenilen kisi ve dayanilir binek gibi bagimli uygulamalari da kapsar.

facets.statement: Temel cekirdek korkuya karsi guven, ic yatiskinligi ve tehlikeden emin olma halidir.
Guven verme, birini kendi koruma ve teminat alani icine alma olarak kullanilir.
Guvenilirlik, ihanete karsi sadakat, emanet edilen sey ve kendisine guvenilen kisi anlamlarini dogurur.
Guvenin bulundugu yer, bir kimsenin emniyet icinde oldugu mesken veya siginak olarak adlandirilir.
Dayanikli ve aksamasindan korkulmayan deve kullanimi, guvenilirlik niteligini canli bir ornege uygular.

branches.source_phrase_ar: الأمن ضد الخوف (ayn;sihah)؛ أصل الأمن طمأنينة النفس وزوال الخوف (mufradat)؛ الأمانة ضد الخيانة ومعناها سكون القلب (maqayis)؛ الأمان إعطاء الأمنة (maqayis;ayn)؛ أمن فلان يأمن أمنا وأمانا وأمنة فهو آمن (tahdhib)؛ استأمن إليه دخل في أمانه (sihah)؛ مأمنه منزله الذي فيه أمنه (mufradat)؛ الأمون الناقة الأمينة الوثيقة أو التي يؤمن فتورها وعثورها (ayn;sihah;mufradat)

branches.what_is_ar: يدخل فيه الإيمان بمعنى التصديق، وتصديق الخبر أو الوعد، والإيمان على سبيل الشريعة أو إذعان النفس للحق حيث نصت المصادر، واستعمال مؤمن بمعنى مصدق الوعد.
يدخل فيه آمين في الدعاء بالمد والقصر، والتأمين بمعنى قول آمين، وتفسيرها باستجب أو اللهم افعل أو كذلك فليكن، مع ذكر قول من جعلها اسما من أسماء الله.

identity_judgment.rationale: Kaynak ifadesi kolu olgunlasmadan sut icme ya da icirme, uygun olmayan yerde kazma veya havuz yapma, suyun alisik olmadigi yere varmasi ve kosulu uygun olmayan hayvan eylemleri gibi somut orneklerle kuruyor. Gecici cerceve bu yersiz veya zamansiz somut islem alanini dogru yansitir.

lexicalization_scope.note: Mekanik kapsam mixed_non_bare oldugu icin sut, toprak, vadi, havuz ve hayvan kaliplari korunur; bunlar ciplak haksizlik anlamina genellenmez.

concept_map.definition: Bir nesne, yer veya canli uzerinde olagan zamanina, yerine ya da kosuluna uymadan yapilan somut islemdir. Sutun olgunlasmadan kullanilmasi, topragin uygunsuz yerde kazilmasi, suyun alisik olmadigi yere varmasi ve gereksiz ya da uygunsuz hayvan eylemleri bu kola baglidir.

facets.statement: Cekirdek, bir somut islemde uygun zaman, yer veya kosulun bozulmasidir.
Sutun olgunlasmadan icilmesi veya icirilmesi zamansiz kullanim ornegidir.
Topragi uygunsuz yerde kazmak, havuzu uygun olmayan yerde yapmak veya vadi suyunun yeni yere ulasmasi yerle ilgili orneklerdir.
Hastalik yokken deveyi kesmek ve gebe disege yaklasan erkek esek canliyla ilgili uygunsuz kosul ornekleridir.

source_synthesis.common_summary: Kaynaklar bu kolu yersiz veya zamansiz somut islem fikri etrafinda toplar. Sutun erken kullanilmasi, uygun olmayan kazma ve havuz yapma, suyun once ulasmadigi yere varmasi ve hayvanlarla ilgili kosul disi eylemler ayni claim icinde birlikte verilir.
